svg.title: Self-attention with trainable Q, K, V weight matrices, building the context vector z squared step by step, with a worked example traced through each step.
svg.desc: Five steps top to bottom: inputs, projection into query/key/value via three learned weight matrices (dk reduced to 2 for readability), scaled dot-product scores, softmax weights, and weighted sum over the value vectors giving context vector z squared = 0.36, 0.60.
svg.text: Self-attention with trainable Q, K, V for x⁽²⁾ (“journey”)
Same flow as before, but weight matrices now sit in front of it — building context vector z⁽²⁾
Each token is a 3-number vector. The example below traces the query x⁽²⁾ meeting x⁽⁵⁾ (“one”).
Step 2 · Project into Q, K, V: q⁽ⁱ⁾=x⁽ⁱ⁾W_q, k⁽ⁱ⁾=x⁽ⁱ⁾W_k, v⁽ⁱ⁾=x⁽ⁱ⁾W_v
These three W matrices are the only learned weights — and the same three are reused for all six tokens.
Note: dₖ = 2 here (3→2) just to keep boxes readable; real LLMs usually keep the dimension the same.
Step 3 · Scaled dot product: ω₂ᵢ = (q⁽²⁾ · k⁽ⁱ⁾) / √dₖ
The query now dots each key (not raw x·x); dividing by √dₖ keeps scores stable as dₖ grows.

g.text: Why divide by √dₖ (the book adds it but doesn’t say why): as dₖ grows, the dot products grow in
magnitude, pushing softmax toward near-0 / near-1 outputs where gradients get tiny. Dividing by √dₖ
keeps the score variance ≈ 1, so training stays stable.

svg.text: Exponentiate each score, divide by the total. Weights are positive and sum to 1.
Step 5 · Weighted sum, the way the code does it: z⁽²⁾ = Σ α₂ᵢ · v⁽ⁱ⁾
Same loop as before, but each pass adds a scaled value vector v⁽ⁱ⁾ (dₖ=2 here), not the raw input.

g.text: for i, v_i in enumerate(values): # values, not raw inputs

svg.text: ↑ after the last += , this is z⁽²⁾
